newsitem.title: USA: Army chief says sex harassment is Army-wide.
newsitem.headline: Army chief says sex harassment is Army-wide.

text.p: The Army's top commander said Wednesday that drill sergeants guilty of rape were exceptional "bad apples" but less serious sex harassment was a widespread problem the Army knew how to fix.
Army Chief of Staff Gen. Dennis Reimer told defence reporters the majority of drill sergeants should not be tarnished by what he called bad apples the Army has always had.

"We've had to deal with those bad apples and we will continue to deal with those bad apples," he said. "... The issue at Aberdeen that bothered me is that we were somewhat surprised by the seriousness of those offences."

Reimer was referring to charges shaking Army ranks that a commander and drill sergeant at the Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland raped women recruits and another drill sergeant had prohibited sex with recruits. All three have denied the charges. Two drill sergeants at Fort Leonard Wood, Mo., have been punished for lesser assaults on recruits and a third was cleared of charges of sexual misconduct.
Reimer said there may be systemic problems at Army training centres, such as too few officers and chaplains for recruits to hear sex misconduct complaints.
He also said higher officers at Aberdeen failed to deal with the drill sergeants' alleged sexual abuse of recruits.
"There was a certain portion of the chain of command that failed. I don't know how much of the chain of command failed. We need to isolate it at those places where the failure took place," he said.

Ultimately, training of Army commanders to spot and deal with sexual harassment -- plus a new "consideration for others" programme -- would solve present widespread sexual harassment in the Army, Reimer said.
"I see sexual harassment as an army-wide problem," he said.
He said that became clear to him when a Defence Department survey released last spring found military women were not confident they could file sex harassment complaints and get action on them.
As a result, he said the Army has been training commanders to be sensitive to sex harassment in their ranks and he expected the training to be completed in March.

He also said the new "consideration for others" programme would be presented to division commanders this spring. He said it would set up meetings between Army men and women to spell out to each other what they consider sex harassment and how to deal with it.
"We're not waiting for some advisory group to tell us what to do. We know what we have to do and we're going about doing it right now," Reimer said.
